newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Nov 6.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Nov 6.

text.p: Prepared by The Broadcast Monitoring Company for Reuters
FINANCIAL TIMES
-- CABINET BOOSTS SPENDING ON HOSPITALS AND SCHOOLS

Following cabinet discussions the government is reported to have agreed to increase the amount of money spent in the fields of education and health next year. The quid pro quo for this rise is a ruling out tax cuts of more than 1p in the pound in the forthcoming Budget, however. The decision is also said to reflect a belief that such spending will produce greater electoral gain than reductions in income tax. The increased spending in some departments will not be met through cuts in others.
-- CABLE TV INDUSTRY ATTACKS BSKYB RATE CARD

The Cable Communications Association has criticised BSkyB over what it sees as efforts to prevent new companies entering into the UK TV and programming fields. The CCA, in a formal response to the Office of Fair Trading on the satellite broadcaster's new rate card for programming, warns that the prices being demanded for programming run counter to consumer and wider industry interests.
-- GEHE OFFERS 650 MILLION STG FOR LLOYDS CHEMISTS

As expected German company Gehe on Tuesday increased its bid offer for Lloyds Chemists. The company has revised its offer up to 650 million stg in cash. The increase, however, remains below the rival offer of 651.3 million stg from UniChem. It had been expected that Gehe would attempt to deliver a knockout blow to UniChem, upping its offer significantly. However, the new Gehe offer was described by the company as "very fair".
-- EU COMPANIES MAY FACE EXTRA TAX FOLLOWING EMU

The federation of European accountants, FEE, has warned that the process of European monetary union could result in some companies experiencing a rise in the amount of tax they pay. The increase will be created by the locking of exchange rates in 1999 and a consequent need for companies to review their long-term assets. The FEE has noted that serious as the issue is, few companies have addressed it fully. The European Commission is also expected to call for greater discussion on the implications for accountancy on general of Emu.
-- BAYER IN TALKS ON DM20 BILLION CHEMICALS ACQUISITION

German chemicals and pharmaceutical company Bayer has announced that it has begun preparations for a large acquisition in the chemicals sector. The company is believed to have begun discussions with Monsanto and Ciba. Both of these companies have revealed plans for a spin-off of their chemicals businesses. Meanwhile, Bayer announced results for the first nine months of the year - with pre-tax profits up 12 per cent to DM3.7 billion.
-- CHANGE IN EU BOND RULES URGED

Investment banks have called for changes to currently tight restrictions on their ability to deal in government bonds. The banks, which would like to see reform take place for the start of Emu, are unhappy with rules in some EU member states that require them to have a local office if they wish to deal in government debt. Such rules add significantly to the operating costs involved.
-- UK, US RESTART OPEN SKIES TALKS

Discussions are due to resume in Washington on Wednesday between British and US representatives on the liberalization of air traffic between the two countries. Previous efforts at securing an open skies policy had collapsed after the UK made it clear it would not enter into the type of agreement reached between the US and other EU states. The US has made an open skies agreement a prerequisite for approval of a tie-up between British Airways and American Airlines.
-- LIABILITY PLANS BROUGHT FORWARD

The British government, in return for agreement to improve the level of financial information disclosed, is reported to be preparing to bring forward plans to allow professionals such as accountants greater protection from claims relating to liability. Such a move would allow accountancy firms to register in Britain as limited liability partnerships. Already a number of major firms have begun considering registering in Jersey, where such protection is now being accorded.
-- FUNDS GET GO-AHEAD DESPITE MPS' FEARS

Despite some concerns about the implications for corporate governance the British government on Tuesday gave its approval to a new form of open ended investment fund. One senior Tory expressed concern that open ended investment companies would not be required to appoint independent directors. There is some speculation that investigations into the recent discrepancies found at Morgan Grenfell Asset Management could result in the new OEICS legislation having to be revised.
-- INDUSTRIAL OUTPUT GROWTH SHOWS RECOVERY SPREADING

Figures from the Office for National Statistics reveal that British manufacturing output grew at a modest rate during October. The figures are seen as an indication that a recovery which till now has mainly been felt in the services sector has finally begun to make itself felt more widely. During the period manufacturing output increased at a seasonally adjusted rate of 0.3 per cent.
